intro: Blurring faces is the polite default before posting a group photo, a class picture, a protest, or a street scene: not everyone in the frame agreed to be online. iPhones with Apple Intelligence gained a way to do this in Photos, but it is limited to recent Pro and 16-series models and certain regions. This guide covers the built-in option, its limits, and a way that works on every supported iPhone.

native.heading: What the Photos app offers
paragraphs: On iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 16 and newer models running iOS 18.1 or later with Apple Intelligence enabled, Photos → Edit → Clean Up lets you brush over a face; the tool pixelates or blurs the covered area. It is manual (one face at a time), the strength is not adjustable, and it is unavailable on older iPhones and in some regions and languages. Without Apple Intelligence, Photos can only cover a face with a Markup shape or sticker — hiding, not blurring.

sections.heading: Automatic face blur for every supported iPhone
paragraphs: How to Blur Photo has a dedicated Faces tab. It detects the faces in the frame and shows them in a grid, each already blurred, so a group photo with a dozen people takes one tap rather than a dozen brush strokes. You choose the style — Pixelate for the classic censored look, Gaussian or Box for a softer one — and Radius for how strong it is. Processing is on-device, which matters when the whole point is privacy.
The requirement is iOS 18.6 or later on any iPhone; there is no dependency on Apple Intelligence hardware.

sections.heading: Blur some faces, keep others
paragraphs: If you want your own face visible and everyone else blurred, use the Manual tab after or instead of Faces: brush over the faces you want hidden and leave yours alone. The same Radius and style apply to the painted area.

sections.heading: How strong is strong enough
paragraphs: A face is still recognisable at low blur, especially to people who know the person. For genuine anonymity, use Pixelate or a Gaussian Radius high enough that eyes, nose, and mouth are indistinguishable at full zoom. The App Store screenshot shows Radius 80 for faces; treat that as a sensible starting point, not a maximum.

intro: The most common “blur” question on Apple’s own forums is about blurring a specific part of a picture: an address in a screenshot, a stranger in the background, a credit card on a table, a child’s school badge. Photos cannot do it — Markup draws shapes, and Clean Up (on Apple Intelligence iPhones) is designed to remove objects, not blur them. Here is what actually works, using the Manual mode in How to Blur Photo.
image_alt: Manual tab in How to Blur Photo used to blur a chosen region

native.heading: The built-in workarounds and their limits
paragraphs: Markup (Photos → Edit → pen icon → + → Add Shape) places a filled rectangle or circle over the area. It hides the content, but it looks like a censor bar and, if you use the highlighter or a low-opacity shape, the detail underneath can still be read. On Apple Intelligence iPhones, Clean Up removes what you brush over, which can leave odd artefacts and does not work on older devices. Neither gives you an actual blur with adjustable strength.

sections.heading: Manual mode: a blur brush for any region
paragraphs: How to Blur Photo’s Manual tab turns your finger into a blur brush. Paint over the region; only the painted area is affected. The style chips decide what kind of blur — Pixelate and Box make text unreadable with a clean, deliberate look; Gaussian gives a soft blur that suits faces and objects; Crystallize and Hexagonal are stylised. Radius controls strength, and the live preview shows exactly what will be saved.
Because you are painting rather than selecting, irregular shapes are easy: a licence plate at an angle, a name badge, a reflection in a window.

sections.heading: Screenshots, documents, and chats
paragraphs: For text, use Pixelate or Box with a Radius high enough that letters are not distinguishable when you zoom in. For a person or object in the background, Gaussian at a moderate Radius looks more natural. In both cases, zoom in before saving — a blur that looks sufficient at thumbnail size is often still readable at full size.

intro: Sharing a screenshot of an order confirmation, a group chat, a ticket, or a document almost always means hiding some text first: a full name, an address, a booking reference, a phone number. Doing it properly matters because a weak blur can be read or even reconstructed. This guide shows the right way on iPhone and the settings that make text unrecoverable.
image_alt: Manual tab with Pixelate style hiding text in How to Blur Photo

native.heading: Why Markup is not enough
paragraphs: Markup’s pen and highlighter are semi-transparent by default, and people regularly share screenshots where the “hidden” text is legible through the stroke. A solid Markup shape at full opacity does hide text, but it looks like a redaction bar and has to be drawn and resized for each line. Clean Up on Apple Intelligence iPhones is built for objects and can produce garbled text rather than removing it.

sections.heading: Pixelate versus blur for text
paragraphs: For text, Pixelate is the better choice. It replaces the area with large blocks, so there is no residual shape to reconstruct, and it visibly communicates “this was hidden on purpose”. Box blur is a close second. Gaussian at a very high Radius also works but needs to be pushed further than people expect; at low Radius the word shapes remain readable. In every case, zoom in before saving.
Radius controls block size for Pixelate. Choose a value where a single block is larger than a letter — for typical screenshot text that means well above 50.

sections.heading: Whole screenshots and multiple lines
paragraphs: If most of a screenshot needs hiding, the Full Photo tab with Pixelate obscures everything, and you can crop afterwards to keep only the relevant part. For a few scattered lines, Manual with a wide brush stroke per line is quicker than shapes in Markup.

sections.heading: Pixelate or Box for plates
paragraphs: Plates are high-contrast text, and high-contrast text is the easiest thing to reconstruct from a weak blur. intro: Pixelation replaces an area with large square blocks. It is the standard way to hide identity or text because it is obvious, clean, and, done properly, irreversible. It is also a look in its own right — retro, 8-bit, glitchy. On iPhone the Photos app cannot pixelate a normal photo; How to Blur Photo makes it a style you can apply to faces, a brushed region, the background, or the whole frame.

native.heading: Pixelate in Photos?
paragraphs: Only via Clean Up on iPhones with Apple Intelligence (iPhone 15 Pro, 16-series and newer, iOS 18.1+), which pixelates or blurs a brushed face with a fixed strength. On other iPhones, and for text or whole-image pixelation, Photos has nothing. Markup shapes cover rather than pixelate.

sections.heading: Block size and Radius
paragraphs: In How to Blur Photo, Radius controls the size of the pixel blocks. Small values give a fine mosaic that hides detail while keeping the general shape; large values give big, obvious squares. For privacy on faces and text, use a block size larger than an eye or a letter. For a retro look on the whole photo, a medium value keeps the scene recognisable.
Pixelate is one of the style chips next to Gaussian, Motion, Ghosting, Box, Hexagonal, and Crystallize. Hexagonal is the same idea with hex cells; Crystallize uses irregular shards.

sections.heading: Four places to pixelate
paragraphs: Faces tab: every detected face is pixelated at once — the App Store listing calls it “pixel privacy in one tap”. Manual tab: brush over a plate, a badge, a screen, or text. Background tab: keep the subject sharp and pixelate everything behind them for a stylised portrait. Full Photo: pixelate the entire image for an abstract or 8-bit version.

h1: Best app to blur background on iPhone — what to use when the photo is already taken
answer: The best app to blur the background on iPhone depends on when you need it: Portrait mode is best before the shot; for photos you already have, a dedicated subject-aware editor such as How to Blur Photo is the practical choice — automatic subject detection, adjustable strength, face and manual modes, free to download, and processed on-device. Markup, Clean Up, and browser tools each solve a different, narrower problem.
intro: “Best app to blur background on iPhone” usually returns a list of ten general photo editors. Most people asking do not want ten editors; they want to know which route gets a sharp subject and a soft background on a photo that is already in their library, without a learning curve or an upload. This page compares the real options — including the ones built into iOS — against that job.
image_alt: How to Blur Photo — sharp subject, blurred background

native.heading: Built-in options first
paragraphs: Portrait mode (Camera): best quality when it works, but only at capture time, only within a couple of metres, and useless for existing photos. Photos f-number slider: adjusts blur on Portrait captures only. Markup: covers areas with shapes; no blur. Clean Up: on Apple Intelligence iPhones, removes objects and can pixelate a brushed face; it does not blur a background. If your photo is already taken in normal mode, none of these blur its background.

sections.heading: What to look for in a background blur app
paragraphs: Automatic subject detection, so you are not tracing outlines with a finger. Adjustable strength, because a headshot and a product photo need different amounts. A manual brush for the cases detection misses. Privacy options (face blur) in the same tool, since the same photos often need both. On-device processing, so personal photos are not uploaded to a server. A price you can see up front.
Web-based blur tools tick some of these boxes but require uploading the photo and typically export a compressed or watermarked file on the free tier.

sections.heading: How to Blur Photo against that list
paragraphs: How to Blur Photo (published under the Make Blur brand) is built around this one job. It detects the subject on the Background tab, has a Radius slider for strength, a Manual tab with a brush, a Faces tab for privacy, and a Full Photo tab. Styles include Gaussian, Motion, Ghosting, Box, Pixelate, Hexagonal, and Crystallize. Processing is on-device with no internet required. It is free to download on iPhone with iOS 18.6 or later; basic background blur is included and advanced styles and tools are in-app purchases ($4.99 and $29.99 on the US store).

What it is not: a general photo editor, a background remover (no transparent cutouts), or a video tool. If you need those, a broader app is the better choice; if you need the background of a photo blurred today, this one is quicker.
